Gryllus (12, madder-red tunic, hair freshly combed) holds a javelin ready to throw at the tree from the ground; several more javelins lie in the grass. Sosias (old Thracian groom, grey beard, weathered face) stands beside a bridled horse, watching closely. grammar.title: Δεῖ, χρή, ἔξεστι, προσήκει · ποιητέον
grammar.rule: τίνα δεῖ ποιεῖν; δεῖ τὸν ἵππαρχον ποιεῖν · τίνι ἔξεστιν; οὐκ ἔξεστί σοι ἀκοντίζειν · τίνι προσήκει; προσήκει τῷ ἱππάρχῳ λέγειν · ποιητέον σοι = δεῖ σε ποιεῖν

tables.caption: -τέον = δεῖ

grammar.note_en:
This chapter is about saying who must, or who may, do something. Greek has two ways of saying ‘must’, and they put the person in different cases. That difference in case is the narrow point of the chapter.

The first way is an impersonal verb: a verb in the third person singular with no real subject, like English ‘it is necessary’. You have read δεῖ and χρή since Athenaze. They take an infinitive for the action and the accusative for the person: «Τί δὲ δεῖ τὸν ἵππαρχον ποιεῖν;» (s010), ‘What must the hipparch do?’, literally ‘it is necessary (for) the hipparch to do what?’. The young hipparch asks the same with χρή: «Τί οὖν χρή με ποιεῖν;» (s059), ‘What then must I do?’. Other impersonal verbs put the person in the dative instead: ἔξεστι ‘it is allowed, it is possible’, προσήκει ‘it is fitting, it is proper’, δοκεῖ ‘it seems good’. Sosias forbids the javelin from horseback with «Οὐκ ἔξεστί σοι ἀπὸ τοῦ ἵππου ἀκοντίζειν» (s091), ‘You are not allowed to throw from the horse’ (literally ‘it is not allowed to you’). Socrates says «καὶ λέγειν εὖ προσήκει τῷ ἱππάρχῳ» (s065), ‘it is also proper for the hipparch to speak well’, and Gryllus says «δοκεῖ γάρ μοι πρῶτον συντάττειν» (s100), ‘for I think it best first to organise them’. So learn each impersonal with its case: δεῖ and χρή with the accusative; ἔξεστι, προσήκει and δοκεῖ with the dative.

The second way is new: the verbal adjective in -τέος, -τέα, -τέον, ‘to be done, needing to be done’. In this chapter it is always the neuter singular -τέον, used like an impersonal verb with ἐστί understood. Socrates’s first demand is «τοὺς ἵππους βελτίους ποιητέον σοι» (s044), ‘you must make the horses better’. It means exactly δεῖ σε ποιεῖν, but the person is now in the dative: σοι, not σε. This is called the dative of agent, the dative of the person who has to do the action. In this chapter’s -τέον examples the person is always dative, and that is the usual pattern; you will sometimes meet an accusative instead, by analogy with δεῖ σε. In the same way «Μελετητέον οὖν τοῖς ἱππεῦσι» (s057) = δεῖ τοὺς ἱππέας μελετᾶν, ‘so the horsemen must practise’, and Gryllus, allowed to throw only from the ground, says «Ἀκοντιστέον οὖν μοι ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς» (s094) = δεῖ με ἀκοντίζειν, ‘so I must throw from the ground’. Xenophon’s own handbook uses the form at once: «ἀναβιβαστέον μέν σοι ἱππέας» (s138), ‘you must mount horsemen’, that is, enlist new riders. These verbs keep their accusative objects: τοὺς ἵππους, ἱππέας.

To recognise the form, look for -τέον (often -ητέον or -στέον) on a verb stem. The stem is usually the one you see in the aorist passive, without its -θ-: ποιη-θῆναι → ποιη-τέον, μελετη-θῆναι → μελετη-τέον, ἀκοντισ-θῆναι → ἀκοντισ-τέον. The -τέον form is always about obligation, never possibility: it never means ‘can’.

So, when you meet ‘must’: with δεῖ or χρή the person is accusative; with -τέον it is usually dative, like the person with ἔξεστι and προσήκει. The meaning does not change; only the case of the person does.

parergon.title: ἔμπειρος, ἄπειρος + γενική
parergon.body_en: Ἔμπειρος ‘experienced’ and ἄπειρος ‘inexperienced’ (ἀ- ‘not’) take a genitive of the thing in which one has or lacks experience, like other adjectives of knowing. Xenophon asks his son «ἔμπειρος εἶ τούτων;» (s071), ‘are you experienced in these things?’, and Gryllus answers «Ἄπειρος νῦν» (s072). Philesia uses the genitive to make her point: «Ἵππαρχος οὖν ἄπειρος τῶν προσόδων καὶ τῶν δαπανῶν καταγέλαστός ἐστιν» (s116), ‘a hipparch inexperienced in income and expenses is ridiculous’. Without a genitive the adjective simply describes a person: «Ὅντινα γὰρ ἂν ἐμπειρότατον νομίζωσι» (s061), ‘whomever they think most experienced’.

families.spelling_note: Both are τάττω ‘put in order, station’ with a preverb, and the augment goes after the preverb: συν-έ-ταξεν (s101), παρ-έ-ταξεν (s099). Παρα- loses its last α before the augment’s vowel; συν- keeps its ν before τ (συν-τάττω) and before the ε of the augment. Attic writes ττ; other dialects and the analyser write σσ (συντάσσω, παρατάσσω). The difference matters in the story. Συντάττω gathers many into one ordered body: Gryllus tries to organise the hounds (s015) and later sets the pebbles in one block. Παρατάττω places a body beside something for battle: Socrates says the horsemen are drawn up παρὰ τὴν φάλαγγα, beside the hoplites’ line (s058), and Diodorus sets his pebble horsemen beside the phalanx he has drawn in the dust. In this chapter’s illustration Gryllus says one must first συντάττειν and then παρατάττειν (s100): first make a unit, then put it in line. Παρατάττω is close to the sum of its parts; it can mean simply ‘place side by side’, but here, as usually in Xenophon, it is a military word: drawing up for battle.
